howItWorks.intro: Stamp duty in Australia isn't one tax — it's eight, one per state and territory, each legislated separately with its own bracket structure, its own thresholds, and its own political appetite for concessions. New South Wales, Victoria, Queensland, Western Australia, South Australia, Tasmania, the ACT and the Northern Territory each run transfer duty through their own Revenue Office or equivalent, so a $750,000 purchase in Sydney and the identical purchase in Melbourne land on different duty bills even before first-home-buyer or foreign-buyer adjustments are applied. What all eight jurisdictions share is the underlying mechanic: duty is charged as a progressive scale against the property's dutiable value (usually the higher of purchase price or market value), with each slice of the price taxed at the rate assigned to that bracket — similar in structure to how income tax brackets work, just applied to a lump sum instead of annual earnings. This calculator applies that bracket logic per state, then layers on the first-home-buyer concession and foreign-buyer surcharge selections so the total reflects the scenario you've entered rather than a flat percentage guess.
rules: Stamp duty is calculated on progressive bands that vary by state/territory
First home buyer exemptions vary by state (e.g., NSW up to $800k, VIC up to $600k)
Foreign buyer surcharges: 7-8% additional on top of standard duty
howItWorks.outro: To see the bracket math in action: take a $750,000 established home in NSW, bought by an Australian citizen who isn't a first-home buyer, using the illustrative NSW-style scale above (1.25% to $17,000, 1.5% from $17,000–$36,000, 1.75% from $36,000–$97,000, 3.5% from $97,000–$364,000, 4.5% from $364,000–$1.21M). Working through each slice: $17,000 × 1.25% = $212.50, plus $19,000 × 1.5% = $285, plus $61,000 × 1.75% = $1,067.50, plus $267,000 × 3.5% = $9,345, plus the remaining $386,000 × 4.5% = $17,370. Add those five slices and the duty comes to roughly $28,280 — an effective rate of about 3.77% of the purchase price, even though no single bracket in the scale is anywhere near 3.77%. That gap between the top marginal bracket and the effective rate is the part of progressive duty scales that catches buyers off guard, the same way it does with income tax. Treat every number on this page — brackets, thresholds, concession caps, surcharge percentages — as illustrative rather than current legislated rates. Stamp duty brackets and first-home-buyer thresholds are amended by state budgets most years (several states index or adjust theirs annually), and a rate that's accurate in one financial year can be superseded within months. Before relying on any figure for an actual settlement, check the current schedule on your state or territory's revenue office website (Revenue NSW, State Revenue Office Victoria, Queensland Revenue Office, and so on) or confirm with your conveyancer or solicitor.

faq.question: How is stamp duty calculated in Australia?
faq.answer: Stamp duty (transfer duty in NSW and some other states) is charged against your property's dutiable value using a progressive bracket scale set by whichever state or territory the property sits in. Instead of one flat percentage, the price is sliced into bands and each band is taxed at its own rate — low bands sit under 2%, the top bands in most states run from roughly 5% to 7% once you're well into seven figures. There's no single 'Australian stamp duty rate': the Northern Territory, Tasmania and the ACT each run materially different scales from NSW or Victoria, so the same purchase price produces different duty bills depending purely on which state the contract is signed in.

faq.question: Do first-home buyers get a stamp duty exemption or concession?
faq.answer: Most states run a first-home buyer scheme, but the mechanics differ enough that 'first home buyer stamp duty' isn't one policy. Some states run a full exemption below one price threshold and a tapering partial concession up to a second, higher threshold; others use a single cliff. Eligibility usually also depends on whether the property is new or established, whether it's owner-occupied within a set period after settlement, and sometimes a value cap that's lower for vacant land than for a finished home. If you select 'Yes' for first-home buyer above, the calculator applies a concession band to the result — check your own state revenue office for the threshold in force this financial year before treating the saved amount as certain.

faq.question: Is there a foreign buyer surcharge, and how is it applied?
faq.answer: Every state and territory adds a surcharge purchaser duty on top of standard transfer duty when the buyer is a foreign person, foreign corporation or foreign trust as defined under that state's Duties Act — the definitions of 'foreign' aren't identical across states, and temporary residents can be caught by rules that permanent residents and citizens aren't. The surcharge is calculated as a flat percentage of the dutiable value and added to the bracket-calculated duty, not blended into the brackets themselves, so it compounds on top of whatever the standard scale produces. Some states also apply a parallel land tax surcharge for foreign owners that's separate from the one-off duty surcharge and charged annually instead.

faq.question: Can stamp duty be added to my home loan?
faq.answer: In practice, no — stamp duty is due to the state revenue office at or shortly after settlement and is expected to come from funds you bring to settlement separately from the loan amount, alongside conveyancing fees, registration fees and any adjustments for rates or water. A handful of lenders will let a low-LVR borrower capitalise duty into the loan, but it's the exception, and doing so increases both your total interest cost and your loan-to-value ratio, which can affect whether lenders mortgage insurance applies. Most first-home buyer budgets treat stamp duty, where it isn't exempted, as a cash cost to save separately from the deposit.

faq.question: Why is the duty on an identical property price different in NSW versus Victoria?
faq.answer: Because transfer duty is state legislation, not federal — each Duties Act sets its own bracket boundaries, its own marginal rates within each bracket, and its own indexing schedule (some states adjust thresholds with CPI or wage growth annually, others only when a budget changes them). Two states can also disagree on what counts as dutiable value, how off-the-plan concessions are structured, or where the top bracket kicks in. That's why a comparison calculator has to hold a state selector as a primary input rather than a secondary detail — the bracket table swapped in behind the scenes is really a different tax, just with a shared name.

faq.question: Does buying off-the-plan or a new build change the duty calculation?
faq.answer: In several states, yes, though the mechanism differs. Some jurisdictions let off-the-plan buyers calculate duty on the contract price minus construction costs not yet incurred at exchange, which can meaningfully lower dutiable value versus a finished home at the same eventual price. Separately, first-home buyer concessions in some states cap higher for new homes than established ones, or apply to new homes only above the property price at which the established-home concession stops, reflecting a state housing-supply incentive rather than a duty-mechanics reason. Vacant land generally follows its own, usually lower-threshold, concession schedule again.

faq.question: When is stamp duty actually due, and what happens if I pay late?
faq.answer: Most states require duty to be paid within a set window after the contract becomes unconditional or at/shortly after settlement — commonly somewhere between 30 and 90 days depending on the state and whether it's an off-the-plan or standard contract. Missing the deadline typically triggers interest calculated daily from the due date plus, in some states, a separate penalty tax component, and unpaid duty can hold up registration of the transfer with the land titles office. In practice most settlements have duty paid by the conveyancer or solicitor out of settlement funds on the day, which avoids the issue, but self-managed or delayed settlements are where the deadline becomes a real risk.

faq.question: Is stamp duty tax-deductible?
faq.answer: Not immediately. For an investment property, stamp duty is generally treated as a capital cost added to the property's cost base for capital gains tax purposes when you eventually sell, rather than an expense you can claim against rental income in the year you buy — it reduces your taxable capital gain down the track instead of your current-year tax bill. Owner-occupied purchases don't get any income-tax offset for duty at all, since the property isn't producing assessable income. Rules around cost base treatment can interact with other deductions and depreciation schedules, so this is worth confirming with a tax agent rather than assuming a blanket answer applies to your structure.
